analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 tax cuts permanent, cuts capital gains to 10%, and ends tax on stock dividends.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single senator in the post-election session with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made permanent the 2001 tax cuts (which were written to expire after 2010) and moved many of them forward sooner: faster income-tax rate cuts, faster and full repeal of the estate tax, a 10% top rate on capital gains, and complete elimination of federal income tax on dividends from publicly traded U.S. companies. It also raised retirement-plan contribution limits ($15,000 for 401(k)s, $5,000 for IRAs) and pushed the age for mandatory retirement-account withdrawals from 70½ to 75. A nonbinding section urged Congress to pass pension safeguards, tort reform, and lighter business regulation. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest dollar gains would have gone to high-income investors and the heirs of very large estates. Repealing the estate tax benefits only the few thousand estates large enough to owe it. Eliminating dividend tax and cutting the capital gains rate to 10% most helps the households that hold most corporate stock and realized gains, which are concentrated at the top. Middle-class savers also would have gained from higher 401(k) and IRA contribution limits and a later mandatory-withdrawal age, and public companies would have gained from a higher stock demand for dividend-paying shares.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset provisions of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, making its tax cuts permanent instead of expiring after 2010.
Accelerates the individual income tax rate reductions so the lower rates arrive sooner, and moves full repeal of the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax up from 2010 to 2005.
Sets a maximum 10% federal tax rate on individuals' net capital gains, down from the then-current top rate of 20%.
Excludes 100% of dividends received from domestic, publicly traded C corporations from taxable income, eliminating the individual-level layer of tax on those dividends.
Raises the deductible IRA contribution to $5,000 and the 401(k) and 457 plan limits to $15,000 immediately, and raises the age at which retirement accounts must begin paying out from 70½ to 75.
Raises the annual deduction limit for individuals' capital losses from $3,000 to $10,000, with inflation indexing.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. Every provision is a revenue loss — permanent rate cuts, an accelerated and permanent estate tax repeal, a 10% capital gains rate, and full dividend exclusion — which would have had to be financed by borrowing or by offsetting cuts elsewhere in the budget. Because the estate tax touches only the largest estates and most stock and dividends are held by top earners, the cost would be spread across all taxpayers while the gains concentrate among the wealthiest.

drawbacks.text: Making the 2001 tax cuts permanent, repealing the estate tax outright, taxing capital gains at 10%, and excluding dividends from income entirely would each be a permanent, open-ended revenue loss for the federal government, at a time when the 2001 law's expiration had been built in precisely to limit its long-term cost.

The dividend exclusion and the estate tax repeal concentrate their benefits at the top of the income and wealth distribution: only the largest estates owe estate tax, and the households holding most dividend-paying stock are high-income.

The bill's nonbinding 'sense of the Senate' section calls for tort reform and for stripping 'outdated regulatory burdens' from business and investors, which signal intent to narrow consumers' and workers' legal remedies and weaken regulatory oversight, though these provisions would have had no force by themselves.

A good-faith supporter would argue the dividend tax amounts to double taxation of corporate profits and that ending it would boost markets and investment; the honest counterweight is that the full exclusion is a poorly targeted way to deliver that relief, since its value scales with the size of one's stock portfolio.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The middle-class pieces are real but small relative to the whole: higher 401(k) and IRA limits and a later withdrawal age genuinely help ordinary savers. But the bulk of the bill's dollar value — a permanent estate tax repeal, a 10% capital gains rate, and zero tax on dividends — flows to the wealthiest households, and all of it is paid for with federal revenue. As designed, the bill was a large, permanent transfer toward concentrated wealth with modest offsets for everyone else, and it offered no way to pay for itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Kyl of Arizona introduced the bill on November 19, 2002, during the Senate's post-election session, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing happened, so no private interest gained or lost anything directly. The public treasury simply kept revenue that a permanent version of these cuts would have erased, and taxpayers avoided the cost of a bill whose heaviest benefits were aimed at the top of the wealth distribution. Notably, versions of the bill's ideas resurfaced in the next Congress: the 2003 tax law adopted a reduced 15% dividend rate rather than the full exclusion this bill proposed, along with accelerated rate and capital gains cuts.

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 19, 2002 and delivered introductory remarks on the floor the next day.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows only a lone Republican sponsor and a committee that never acted.

industries.industry: Wealthy households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: The bill would have accelerated full estate tax repeal to 2005 and made it permanent; only the few thousand estates large enough to owe the tax pay it. The public cost is the lost revenue, spread across all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Asset managers, brokers, and high-income shareholders
industries.note: A zero rate on dividends and a 10% capital gains rate raise after-tax returns on stock, increasing demand for investment products and advisory fees. Small savers gain something too, but because stock ownership is concentrated at the top, the bulk of the value goes to wealthy households.
Exempting their dividends from individual tax would make their shares more valuable and cheaper to finance. Ordinary small shareholders would share in this, though the largest holders gain the most.
The bill's nonbinding section calls for 'meaningful tort reform,' which if enacted later would narrow lawsuits against businesses. It would have carried no legal force on its own.
